The thinnest set in Unicode

H₂O and CO₂ are the reason this set exists. Unicode carries subscript characters so a formula can survive in a plain-text field, not so an entire sentence can be lowered, and the coverage reflects that narrow purpose. There are no subscript capitals whatsoever, and only about seventeen lowercase letters have one: a e h i j k l m n o p r s t u v x. Everything else arrives exactly as typed. The digits ₀ to ₉ are all present.

Set against the superscript range, which at least has most of an alphabet, this is the thinnest style on the site, and a word run through it usually returns half lowered and half not. That is fine for what it is good at: an index like xₙ, a variable in a forum post about physics, a lab note in a field with no equation editor. The lowered characters are separate letters rather than a formatting switch, so no editor can strip them later.

Also searched as: chemistry formula text, small text below, lowered numbers, index text.

Where Subscript text works, and where it does not

WorksReads as ordinary text everywhere, because these are normal Unicode letters rather than a maths alphabet. Watch outUnicode has no character for every letter in this style, so the missing ones stay plain. That is the honest fallback, not a fault.

Subscript questions

Why can I not lower a capital letter?

There are no subscript capitals in Unicode, none at all. The set was added for scientific notation, where indices and formulae are written with lowercase letters and digits, so capitals were never encoded. If you need something like a capital N as an index, the usual workaround is to use its lowercase form.

How do I write a chemical formula?

Type it normally and lower only the counts: H, then a subscript two, then O. Because the digits nought to nine are all present, any formula built on numbers works completely, which covers most of chemistry. Ionic charges are the awkward case, since those want raised characters from the superscript set instead.

Can I mix lowered and normal text in one line?

That is the normal case here and the generator assumes it. Anything with no subscript character available passes through at full size rather than being dropped, so a sentence comes back part lowered and part plain. For a variable with an index, run only the index through and leave the letter alone.
